items.heading: Search "How to Choose Search
items.text: Search "How to Choose Search Search "How to Choose Search "how to choose a career" and most advice assumes you already have some work history to draw on, full control over your own money, and years of adult life to test things out. None of that is true for a teenager, and pretending otherwise is why so much of that advice feels like it does not fit.

items.heading: Name the Real Cost Name
items.text: Name the Real Cost Name the real cost. Money, time, anything you are asking them to rearrange. A specific, small number is easier to say yes to than an open-ended request.

items.heading: If You Are Still
items.text: If you are still a few years out from choosing a stream, your only real job right now is to widen the input and practise finishing things. Not to know your career. Sample subjects, hobbies, small responsibilities, and clubs on purpose, and pay attention to what you keep returning to without being told to.

visuals.heading: The Proof Gap: You Do Not Have

columns: Why it does not fully work
rows: What do you keep doing without anyone assigning it: a subject you reread for fun, a hobby you return to, a problem you keep poking at. This one works at any age.
The adult version needs colleagues or managers who have watched you work professionally - you do not have that yet.

Ask a teacher, coach, club sponsor, tuition mentor, or family friend who has actually supervised you on something specific: "What is one thing you would trust me to handle without checking twice?" Write down the exact words. A skill three different adults name unprompted is real evidence.
The adult version needs real employers or clients currently paying for the exact combination - that requires an income history you are not yet old enough to have built.

Use the closest honest substitute: a competition, olympiad, or hackathon result judged by outsiders, a small paid task like tutoring a junior or helping run a stall, a tiny freelance job for a local business, or one day shadowing someone in the field and asking what a beginner is actually expected to know.
Transfers directly, with one condition: it has to be tested against a real task, not the idea of the job.
Notice which parts of a school project, hobby, or small responsibility you keep choosing to do again versus the parts you quietly avoid, even when you are capable of both.

items.heading: Name the Smallest Test, Not
items.text: Name the smallest test, not the whole plan. Not "I want to become a game designer." Instead: "I want to spend one weekend building a small game in a free tool and show you what I made.".

items.heading: Name What Happens If IT
items.text: Name what happens if it does not work. You go back to the current plan with no argument about it. This is the line that turns a fear-based "no" into a low-risk "try it.".

items.heading: Set a Date to Show
items.text: Set a date to show them what you built. A specific date to sit down and look at the actual result, not a vague promise to "figure it out." This is what makes a parent trust the next ask.

items.heading: That a Stream Picked Under
items.text: That a stream picked under pressure at 15-16 with no real testing usually gets carried three or four more years out of sunk cost, not fit.

items.heading: That "Figuring IT Out Later"
items.text: That "figuring it out later" almost always means figuring it out at a much more expensive, much less reversible moment - after a degree, not before one.

items.heading: That a Teenager Who Has
items.text: That a teenager who has never tested a real task has no evidence yet about what the daily work of any option actually feels like.
